cards.title: SDF vs. MSDF vs. Slug: GPU Text Rendering

depth.text: someone explains how **Slug** keeps **GPU text** sharp without baking letters into an image

Slug stores **glyph outlines** and calculates coverage in a **fragment shader**, skipping a texture atlas and per-frame tessellation. The article says this keeps text crisp through extreme scaling and perspective, while some commenters argue **MSDF plus raster fallback** may be simpler and good enough.

cards.camps: Two camps: Slug fans praise its perspective rendering; MSDF users say MSDF plus raster fallback may be simpler and good enough.

comments.text: Slug mentioned! When the Slug patent was released to the public domain, I put together[1] Snail[2], a Slug implementation in Zig. One thing I found was that it was tough to get small text to look good with some fonts. TrueType fonts often have bytecode that tweaks curve points to better fit the pixel grid at a particular size. Part of the pitch for Slug is that it doesn't require per-size glyph…

I once implemented SDF text rendering. To me, the thing I liked the most about this technique it how easy it is to add effects on top. With a few lines of shader code, I had outlines and softening of the edges (antialiasing). I didn't try the MSDF variant, as I didn't mind corners not being sharp when scaled up, so I don't know if these effects break on MSDF. Slug doesn't seem to support any of…

This article has some inaccurate information since MSDF atlas doesn't have to be baked statically, so the "CJK character means huge atlas" is not really an issue if you can async upload them to the atlas.（Async outline extraction is a bit harder for C libraries, so that's why the pipeline is mostly restricted to atlas upload). The other thing is MSDF rendering is fairly cheap and can be done on…

I've also been working on a GPU curve renderer, Windfoil, based on a formulation that Fable 5 originally proposed to me during a directed search [1]. It is similar in some ways to Slug, not always as fast, but uses less shader storage (single band instead of two) and produces higher quality anti-aliasing i.e. closer to a box-filtered ground truth. It may be of interest to some game/graphics devs…

cards.title: Burning Man death rates – A short lesson in statistics

depth.text: someone compares **Burning Man’s death rate** with **US population statistics**, and commenters question the math

A commenter says the author compares **3 deaths** at Burning Man with **4.9 expected** from the age-adjusted US death rate. Others argue **selection bias** makes that comparison shaky: people who are seriously ill are less likely to go.

cards.camps: Some commenters call it a great article; others argue selection bias and the 4.9-versus-3 gap make the comparison unreliable.

comments.text: Some of this is selection bias, but lots of this is active work by the organizers. Burning Man has slowly re-created the regulatory state in response to the standard pressures of civilization. To their credit, this has often been in response to near-misses, but sometimes in response to fatalities. It started with sanitation (potties), and banning guns/explosives. You can have 100 people shooting…

Looking at population-level statistics, even adjusted for age, is useless. Going to burning man requires a level of health, energy, free time (not dealing with health issues), and freedom from chronic illnesses that make traveling to a desert a bad idea. Most people at high risk of random death are filtered out before they arrive. There are so many better comparisons that could have been chosen…

Brent Chapman, author of "Incident Management for DevOps and SRE", just got back from his annual "not exactly a vacation" trip to Burning Man, where he's worked as a "Dispatch Supervisor" since 2012.[1] I as able to hear him at BayLISA giving his talk on incident command and what we can learn from the fire department[2][3], an excellent talk. [1]…

The biggest factor is selection bias. If you are in the hospital with some terrible medical condition you aren’t going to Burning Man. It would be interesting to look at cause of death at Burning Man, I would expect it to differ significantly from the population overall (even accounting for age).

One point that I haven't seen mentioned here is that deaths that happen outside of the event boundaries are not "counted." For example, if someone is medevac'ed and dies en route or in a Reno hospital, the event organizers don't include that fatality in their count. There may be a distinction as to who is legally allowed to declare someone dead, and whether that can occur on-playa. Road…

cards.title: What TLA+ can and can't check

depth.text: an explainer says **formal checks** catch many bugs, but can't prove **every useful property**

TLA+ requires checked properties to hold for **every behavior**, so it can't directly ask whether a state is **reachable** or compare two behaviors—a limit for **security and statistical properties**. You can mimic some of this with auxiliary variables or self-composition, but those hacks can make models messy or much larger.

cards.camps: Two camps: the article says TLA+ can't express reachability directly; one commenter says a failed invariant can indirectly show that a winning state is reachable.

comments.text: While both TLA+ and ADA/Spark might be necessary, I haven’t noticed much mention of ADA/SPARK here, which kind of surprised me that they are not used in conjunction as frequent as I might have thought. For some critical software we developed, we used TLA+ for high-level formal specification. As mentioned earlier, transitioning the actual implementation to another language can be challenging…

I discovered Quint[0] due to this comment[1] on HN. Quint is "an executable specification language [which works in JavaScript] with delightful tooling based on the temporal logic of actions (TLA)". I think it is awesome and anybody interested in TLA+ should check it out. [0]: https://github.com/quint-co/quint [1]: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49865720

I love this. This is great to read if you are trying to use TLA+ for something. In a different vein, another thing TLA+ isn't great at is modeling atomics and in particular weak-memory semantics or anything that's not sequentially consistent. If you translate your algorithm to pcal, it will run as if it was sequentially consistent. If you need to model non-sequential-consistency, then that needs…

Great write-up. People keep saying "we can just write tests" or more recently "we can use formal verification," thinking these are sufficient safeguards we can use and then relegate all the implementation to LLMs. But the fact is that probabilistic guessing machines can't save them. People can't escape the need to actually understand the things they are building.

i think part of this is a shortcoming of our programming languages. generally, languages allow for the expression of partial graphs, which makes the verification problem technically challenging. my take is that a language that only exposes closed-graph semantics could help bridge the gap between the model and the implementation, even if not absolute.

cards.title: Why the Bronze Age Collapsed

depth.text: the article says **local iron** put weapons in more hands and made **empires harder to rebuild**

Bronze depended on **tin from distant deposits**; iron could be **smelted locally**, giving peripheral communities weapons comparable to imperial elites. The article also cites records showing average reign lengths in Assyria, Babylon and Athens fell 29 percent after iron’s adoption.

cards.camps: Two camps: the article says local iron made empires harder to rebuild; some commenters say bronze-trade disruption came first, while others argue several causes mattered.

comments.text: Eric Cline makes a good case that the Bronze Age empires were organized around a “palace economy”, where only certain people (royals & their pals) were even allowed to trade. In some places the sovereign literally owned all the land and people on it. One can imagine that a series of bad seasons, natural disasters, invasions & other stressors would open a window for revolt. Yes tin was a factor…

The Bronze Age collapsed for many reasons but the event that really kicked things off was the explosion of Santorini. The empires that died were not quickly replaced because after extensive famines and invasions they were replaced by different people with different social objectives. The same thing happened later in Europe when Germanic and Asian tribes displaced the Roman and Celtic tribes of…

Well, doesn’t the Harappan civilization make a mess out of all this? Tin was nearby, and there’s evidence of bronze artifacts in all kinds of houses across the cities, and in general less evidence of hierarchical power, and certainly nothing like the concentration you see in other Bronze Age civilizations. We don’t have the civilization surviving as is to the Iron Age, because it depopulated…

cards.title: Surprisingly complex waves reveal the brain's inner workings

depth.text: scientists found **brain waves** can form **spirals and ripples** during memory tasks, not just simple patterns

Using **intracranial electrodes**, researchers saw concentric waves and rotating spirals during memory tasks; spirals appeared more often during the harder **spatial task**. Scientists still disagree about whether these patterns help organize brain activity or simply reflect what neurons are already doing.

cards.camps: Two camps: some researchers think traveling waves help coordinate or reorganize brain activity; György Buzsáki says they merely reflect activity happening at the synaptic level.
entities: Shenzhen Medical Academy of Research and Translation

cards.title: Tesla takes on $30B in credit as it approaches unprofitability

depth.text: Tesla has opened **credit lines** as **profits fall** and spending on future projects rises

A filing shows **$30 billion** in loan facilities from **Citi and Wells Fargo**, with terms between one and five years, replacing a previous $5 billion credit line. Tesla says it doesn’t expect to draw on the line in 2026, while planning **$25 billion** in spending that year.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say Tesla squandered its lead with weak products and big promises; others say Electrek’s coverage is biased against Tesla and Musk.

cards.title: 5x faster Edge Functions: V8 isolates to Firecracker MicroVMs

depth.text: Netlify says **Edge Functions** are about **five times faster** after moving them onto its own network

Warm invocations now cost **~5–6ms at median**, down from **25–40ms** on the previous infrastructure. Each function runs in its own **Firecracker MicroVM**, and requests stay inside Netlify’s network.

cards.camps: Two camps: skeptics say Netlify may have removed network hops rather than made execution faster; others say the old hosted runtime explains the latency and MicroVMs offer stronger isolation.

comments.text: I've been using SlicerVM extensively - which is Firecracker MicroVMs for the regular person (and for the irregular with their platform offering) - to run local 'edge' style workloads locally and securly. Agents, local dev CI, etc. It slotted in and replaced my proxmox vm orchestrator, and now I have secure and and fast vms on my laptop wherever I go. It also supports dockerfile style builds if…

Alex from Unikraft here! Happy to answer any questions about the microVM part of the story from our side. We also did a couple of technical write ups if you're interested: - https://unikraft.com/blog/netlify-edge-functions - https://unikraft.com/customer-stories/edge-functions-netlify

> In the past, requests went out to a hosted execution service. Today, they run on MicroVMs inside our own edge network — roughly 5x faster at the median. So, the execution itself might now be slower as far as we know, they just eliminated some networking from the mix? Misleading.
I'm having trouble understanding/believing this, given that Cloudflare Workers are also v8 isolates and run vastly faster than the 25-40ms that netlify says their isolates took...

All else being equal, v8 isolates should be lower latency than firecracker. As they mention, the v8 latency was because the v8 runtime was hosted externally. Firecracker has better security model. This old thread[0] with kentonv author of Cloudflare's workers platform covers some of the differences. [0]: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=31740885
